new_statements.quote: [p. 17] In Uyghur, being a Turkic lexical stress in Turkic language, typically stress occurs on the final syllable of a word (Muti, 2007), in polysyllabic words of Turkic origin. Therefore, Uyghur is known as a final stress language. However, sometimes stress is not in final position in Uyghur. For example, some negation suffixes and enclitics do not attract stress, and stress falls in non-final position (Muti, 2007: 43). These exceptions usually occur in non-Turkic borrowings or in Turkic words that originated from different word classes. [p. 125] Uyghur does not use pitch for distinguishing stress accent. This research suggests that Uyghur is not a pitch-accent language.

new_statements.relation_note: Agrees with the catalog's final-stress rule (StressTyp2: final stress) as the default and adds detail: pre-stressing negation suffixes/enclitics, lexically fixed non-final stress in loans and a handful of minimal pairs, duration (not F0) as the phonetic correlate, and the explicit rejection of a pitch accent analysis.
new_statements.rule_in_words: Default word stress on the final syllable of polysyllabic words of Turkic origin. Exceptions: certain negation suffixes and enclitics do not attract stress (stress stays on the syllable before them, cf. Muti 2007: 43), and non-Turkic (Arabic/Persian) loans and some Turkic words that lost syllables historically carry lexically fixed non-final stress, so a small set of stress minimal pairs exists (Acha 'elder sister' vs aCHA 'branching', BAla 'child' vs baLA 'disaster', TÖshük 'kitchen' vs töSHÜK 'hole', DAka 'gauze' vs daLA 'plain'). Acoustically the stressed syllable is cued by duration (intensity weaker, moderated by CV vs CVC), never by F0; the author concludes Uyghur is a stress-accent, not a pitch accent, language.
new_statements.exceptions: Pre-stressing negation suffixes and enclitics (stress non-final, Muti 2007: 43); non-Turkic borrowings and Turkic words of other word classes / with historical syllable loss carry non-final stress; six stress minimal pairs (Table 4, p. 38), one member of most pairs being a loan or a reduced older form; native speakers are 'often' inconsistent in assigning stress across speakers (p. 52), and the standard dictionary (Yakup & Gheyurani 1999) marks no stress (p. 53); syllable weight is raised as a possible factor because of the Arabic loan stratum but tested only as CV vs CVC, with an effect on duration cues, not on placement (pp. 50, 106).
new_statements.identity_note: The work describes Modern Standard Uyghur (ISO 639-3 uig) as spoken by five native speakers from Xinjiang living in Kansas (context sentences reference Kashgar); no dialect-specific claim is made, though it notes some minimal-pair members are regional or archaic (e.g. TÖshük 'kitchen').

tone_statements.quote: [§6.7, p. 34-35] In this chapter, we have presented a preliminary model of the intonational phonology of Uyghur. We have presented evidence that duration is the most reliable indicator of prominence in Uyghur words, in line with Yakup (2013). Furthermore, f0 does not associate with prominent syllables, but rather with the edges of phrases. As such, Uyghur appears to be a language with prosodic heads that are ignored by the intonational system. [§6.3, p. 5] This suggests that although Uyghur can be described as a stress language, stress and intonational tone are independent.

tone_statements.quote: Uyghur exhibits only edge-marking intonation (Yakup 2013, Major and Mayer 2018). There are three levels of prosodic constituents whose edges may bear tonal targets. [...] The lowest prosodic level whose edges may bear tones is the accentual phrase (AP). An AP is marked on its left edge by a L tone, and a H target (Ha) on its right edge. [...] The next prosodic level is the intermediate phrase (ip), which is marked by a high tone (H-) on its right edge. [...] the highest level is the intonational phrase (IP), which is marked by either a low (L%) or high (H%) tone on its right edge.

sources.quote: 'The status of phonemic vowel length and stress in Uyghur is somewhat unclear'; Yakup 2013 / Yakup & Sereno 2016 show stress reflected only in duration and 'Uyghur speakers frequently disagreed as to which syllables were stressed in many words'; Major & Mayer attribute pitch contours to phrasal prosody. sources.citation: Yakup, Mahire & Joan A. Sereno. 2016. Acoustic correlates of lexical stress in Uyghur. Journal of the International Phonetic Association 46(1): 61-77. doi:10.1017/S0025100315000183 (author-lab copy, kuppl.ku.edu).
sources.quote: Earlier Chinese acoustic studies (Liang & Zhang 2008; Jiang et al. 2010) 'assumed that stress would fall on the final syllable'. Treats Uyghur stress as lexically contrastive in a small set of disyllabic minimal pairs (Table 1: ˈaʧa 'elder sister' vs aˈʧa 'branching', ˈbala 'child' vs baˈla 'disaster', ˈara 'fork' vs aˈra 'between' ...); 'Uyghur stress is not well understood (explanations invoke vowel length, syllable structure, and location in the stem)'; across three experiments duration, not f0 or intensity, cues stress. Note: marks 'child' as ˈbala (initial) where Nadzhip 1971:63 gives bal

sources.note: First-hand acoustic + AM analysis: Uyghur has no lexical tone and no pitch accents; word stress (cued by duration only) is ignored by the intonational system; all tones are post-lexical edge tones - AP melody L H L Ha (AP-internal LHL optional), ip boundary H-, IP boundary L%, H%, HL%, LH% (Table 6.4 'Inventory of tones found in Uyghur'). Typologically rare: a stress language with only edge-marking intonation.

sources.note: Speech-corpus study (Xinjiang University) of sentence-level pitch contours of four standard-Uyghur imperative sentences split into 'tone groups' (prosodic phrases), using Shi Feng's undulating-scale method. Section 2 (p. 222) opens: 'Uyghur language is not a tonal language, so the convenience of studying, we designed following a relatively simple and typical four imperative sentences'. Finds overall falling contours with slight final rise; no lexical tone; word stress mentioned only in passing ('stressed syllable lengthening', p. 227).
